source_refs.note: Chapter 17 exercise (PDF 81-82), solved: 7 MCQs keyed from the chapter's text, 7 short (Q7: five pairs as tables), 4 long and 3 inquisitive questions with model answers. No answer key is printed. MCQ 3 and 5 and Short Q2 carry Book corrections.

blocks.prompt: 1. Fertilization of the ovum occurs in:
blocks.explanation: The ovum enters the oviduct after ovulation; fertilization occurs there and the zygote divides while still in the oviduct (17.1.2).

blocks.prompt: 2. Which cells of the testis secrete testosterone hormone?
blocks.explanation: LH stimulates Leydig cells, in the interstitial tissue between the seminiferous tubules, to secrete testosterone; Sertoli cells nourish developing sperms (17.1.1).

blocks.prompt: 3. The site of the production of sperm is:
blocks.explanation: Spermatogenesis takes place in the germinal epithelium of the seminiferous tubules of the testes; the epididymis only stores and matures them (17.1.1).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: Option (d) prints "Vas deference"; the tube is the vas deferens.

blocks.prompt: 4. Which part produces fructose-rich fluid for the sperm?
blocks.explanation: Each seminal vesicle releases a fluid rich in fructose that provides energy for the sperm (17.1.1).

blocks.prompt: 5. In males, which hormone initiates spermatogenesis?
blocks.explanation: FSH from the anterior pituitary stimulates the seminiferous tubules for spermatogenesis; LH acts on Leydig cells (17.1.1).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: Option (b) is printed with the label "b)" without its opening bracket; it is option (b), a print slip only.

blocks.prompt: 6. During ovulation which cell is actually released from ovary?
blocks.explanation: At puberty a primary oocyte completes meiosis I to form a secondary oocyte, which stops in metaphase II and is ovulated; it completes meiosis II only if a sperm fuses with it (17.1.2).

blocks.prompt: 7. Which hormone stimulates the Graafian follicle to release ovum?
blocks.explanation: The sudden release of LH from the anterior pituitary on day 14 stimulates the Graafian follicle to release the ovum (ovulation) (17.1.2).

blocks.prompt: 1. Briefly describe the function of seminal vesicles, prostate gland, and bulbourethral glands.
blocks.explanation:
These accessory glands add fluids to sperms to form semen.
1. Seminal vesicles: release a fructose-rich fluid into the vas deferens, which gives energy to sperms.
2. Prostate gland: produces about 60% of the fluid of semen.
3. Bulbourethral glands: secrete a clear fluid that lubricates the urethra and gives a protective neutral environment to sperms.

blocks.prompt: 2. When do the ova in a females begin meiosis? When do they complete the first meiotic division?
blocks.explanation:
Meiosis begins during the embryonic development of the female: oogonia divide by mitosis into primary oocytes, which begin meiosis I but stop in prophase I and stay so through childhood.
Meiosis I is completed after puberty, in one primary oocyte each cycle (before ovulation), giving a secondary oocyte and the first polar body.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The question prints "the ova in a females"; it should read "the ova in a female" (or "in females").

blocks.prompt: 3. Write a brief note on the role of FSH, LH and testosterone in man.
blocks.explanation:
GnRH from the hypothalamus makes the anterior pituitary release FSH and LH.
1. FSH stimulates the seminiferous tubules for spermatogenesis (and Sertoli cells to release inhibin, which inhibits further FSH).
2. LH stimulates Leydig cells to secrete testosterone.
3. Testosterone stimulates development of the germinal epithelium, is needed for sperm production and maintains male secondary sexual characteristics; it inhibits further LH and GnRH (negative feedback).

blocks.prompt: 4. List the structures of female reproductive system.
blocks.explanation:
1. Gonads: two ovaries (with ovarian follicles).
2. Oviducts (fallopian or uterine tubes).
3. Uterus: fundus, body and cervix; wall of perimetrium, myometrium and endometrium.
4. Vagina.
Oviducts, uterus and vagina are the accessory organs.

blocks.prompt: 5. What changes occur in ovulation and menstruation during gestation period.
blocks.explanation: Both stop during gestation (pregnancy). The embryo secretes human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG), which maintains the corpus luteum, so estrogen and progesterone stay high (later the placenta also makes progesterone). High progesterone keeps the endometrium thick, so menstruation does not occur, and it inhibits FSH, so no new follicles ripen and ovulation is suppressed.

blocks.prompt: 6. What is the role of the corpus luteum in a menstrual cycle?
blocks.explanation: After ovulation, LH turns the ruptured Graafian follicle into the yellow corpus luteum. It secretes estrogen and progesterone, which make the endometrium more vascular and glandular for implantation (secretory phase). If fertilization does not occur, it degenerates; estrogen and progesterone fall and the endometrium is shed (menstruation on day 28).

blocks.prompt: 1. Describe the structure of human male reproductive system. Identify the function of each part.
blocks.explanation:
1. Gonads (testes): two oval testes (3-5 cm × 2-3 cm) in the scrotum outside the abdomen (kept at about 34°C, needed for sperm development). Each is made of coiled seminiferous tubules; their germinal epithelium has germline cells (make sperms by meiosis) and Sertoli cells (nourish sperms). Leydig cells between tubules secrete testosterone.
2. Accessory ducts: rete testis (network receiving sperms) → epididymis (long coiled tube; sperms stay at least 18 hours and become motile) → vas deferens (passes into the abdomen via the inguinal canal) → joins the duct of the seminal vesicle to form the ejaculatory duct → the two ejaculatory ducts pass through the prostate and open into the urethra, which carries sperms (and urine) out through the penis.
3. Accessory glands (form semen): seminal vesicles (fructose-rich fluid giving energy), prostate gland (about 60% of semen fluid), bulbourethral glands (clear fluid lubricating the urethra, neutral protective environment).
4. Copulatory organ (penis): contains urethra, erectile tissue, an artery and two veins; delivers sperms into the female tract.

blocks.prompt: 2. Explain the major reproductive hormones of human male and explain their role.
blocks.explanation:
Spermatogenesis and male reproduction are controlled by hormones of the hypothalamus, pituitary and testes:
1. Gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH), from the hypothalamus: stimulates the anterior pituitary to release FSH and LH.
2. Follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH): stimulates the seminiferous tubules for spermatogenesis.
3. Luteinizing hormone (LH): stimulates Leydig cells (interstitial tissue) to secrete testosterone.
4. Testosterone (an androgen): stimulates development of the germinal epithelium and is needed for normal sperm production; matures the male reproductive organs; produces and maintains male secondary sexual characteristics and sex drive.
5. Inhibin (peptide from Sertoli cells, released under FSH): inhibits further FSH secretion.
Negative feedback: inhibin limits FSH, and testosterone inhibits the release of LH and GnRH, so hormone levels stay balanced.

blocks.prompt: 3. Explain the structures of human female reproductive system. Identify the function of each part.
blocks.explanation:
1. Ovaries (gonads): two oval ovaries (3-5 cm × 2-3 cm), one on each side of the uterus. They produce egg cells and hormones (estrogen, progesterone). They contain ovarian follicles, the functional units that nurture immature eggs; each month one follicle releases its egg (ovulation) and becomes the corpus luteum.
2. Oviducts (fallopian/uterine tubes): two tubes from the ovaries to the uterus; receive the ovum, move it by cilia towards the uterus; site of fertilization and the first mitotic divisions of the zygote.
3. Uterus: hollow muscular organ with fundus (top), body (main part) and cervix (narrow lower part opening into the vagina). Wall: perimetrium (outer thin layer), myometrium (thick smooth muscle), endometrium (inner spongy lining with a basal layer of stem cells and a functional layer that thickens and is shed in each cycle). It receives and implants the embryo; its vascular spaces form the placenta, which supplies oxygen and food to the foetus.
4. Vagina: thin-walled 8-10 cm tube from the cervix to the outside; passage for delivery of the baby and menstrual flow.

blocks.prompt: 4. Describe the events of a menstrual cycle and explain its hormonal regulation.
blocks.explanation:
The menstrual cycle is the cyclic series of events of the female reproductive system, about 28 days long.
1. Menstrual phase (days 1-5): low estrogen and progesterone cause the functional layer of the endometrium to be shed with blood (menstruation, 3-5 days). FSH begins to rise.
2. Proliferative phase and ovulation (days 6-14): rising FSH makes a few follicles grow; only one becomes the Graafian follicle, which rises to the ovary surface. FSH makes it secrete estrogen, which vascularises the endometrium and makes it thick again. Rising estrogen lowers FSH (negative feedback), and the anterior pituitary releases a surge of LH at day 14, which makes the Graafian follicle release the ovum into the oviduct (ovulation).
3. Secretory (post-ovulatory) phase (days 15-28): LH turns the ruptured follicle into the corpus luteum, which secretes estrogen and progesterone, making the endometrium more vascular and glandular. If fertilization does not occur, the corpus luteum degenerates, LH stops, estrogen and progesterone fall abruptly and the endometrium is shed (menstruation on day 28); the cycle starts again.
If the ovum is fertilized, the embryo secretes hCG, which maintains the corpus luteum, keeps estrogen and progesterone high and prevents menstruation. The cycle stops at about 50 years (menopause).

rows: Low estrogen and progesterone; endometrium shed; FSH starts rising
FSH grows Graafian follicle; estrogen rebuilds endometrium; LH surge on day 14 causes ovulation
LH forms corpus luteum; estrogen + progesterone make endometrium glandular; fall in both causes menstruation

blocks.prompt: 1. List the structures in order, through which a sperm passes on its way from the seminiferous tubules to the outside.
blocks.explanation: Seminiferous tubules → rete testis → epididymis → vas deferens → ejaculatory duct (through the prostate gland) → urethra (in the penis) → outside.

blocks.prompt: 2. Describe the effect of endocrine disrupting contaminants on the reproductive abilities.
blocks.explanation:
(Beyond the chapter.) Endocrine-disrupting contaminants are chemicals in the environment (e.g. some pesticides such as DDT, plasticisers such as bisphenol A and phthalates, dioxins, heavy metals) that mimic or block natural hormones. Since reproduction is controlled by GnRH, FSH, LH, testosterone, estrogen and progesterone, these chemicals upset that balance:
1. In males: lower testosterone, lower sperm count and quality, and abnormal development of reproductive organs.
2. In females: irregular menstrual cycles and ovulation, early puberty, and reduced fertility.
3. During pregnancy: they can harm the developing foetus and its reproductive organs, and increase miscarriage.
So they reduce the reproductive ability (fertility) of people and wildlife.

blocks.prompt: 3. Why are so many sperms produced in the male and so few ova produced in the female?
blocks.explanation:
Sperms: spermatogenesis is continuous from puberty and one spermatogonium gives four sperms. Very many are needed because most die or are lost on the long journey through the female tract (beyond the chapter: acidity, distance, immune attack), and many sperms are needed to help one reach and penetrate the ovum; the sperm is tiny and cheap to make.
Ova: all primary oocytes are formed before birth and only one matures each month; one primary oocyte gives only one ovum (the rest of the cytoplasm is kept for it, the polar bodies degenerate). The ovum is large and stores food, and the uterus can usually support only one embryo at a time, so few large ova are produced.
